headline: High-risk default interaction: Cursor can ingest ChatGPT Desktop outputs via clipboard/files while both can touch user data, creating prompt-injection, leakage, and cascading-action exposure.

A_prompt_injection.rationale: ChatGPT Desktop can expose content through clipboard, files, and Work-with-Apps, while Cursor reads clipboard contents and workspace files. That creates a plausible default bridge where attacker-controlled text from A can be pasted or opened in B and treated as instructions. No shared MCP is shown, so I do not escalate to high.
conditions: IF ChatGPT Desktop content is copied into Cursor without sanitization, prompt injection is possible.
IF Cursor opens files exported from ChatGPT Desktop as trusted instructions, malicious directives can be followed.
mitigations: Disable clipboard-based handoff between the apps.
Use a plain-text sanitizer before pasting into Cursor.
Keep ChatGPT Desktop outputs in separate files from code workspaces.
Review any pasted instructions line-by-line before execution.

B_data_leakage.rationale: A touches uploaded files, screenshots, voice, and connected IDE code, while B touches source code, open files, and clipboard contents. Because both can read local content and B can write to the workspace, sensitive material can move from A into B’s context or outputs in default workflows. The profiles do not show a guaranteed exfiltration path beyond vendor APIs, so medium fits.
conditions: IF sensitive files are opened in ChatGPT Desktop and then copied into Cursor, leakage occurs.
IF Cursor indexes or transmits open files containing secrets, those secrets enter B's backend context.
mitigations: Keep secrets out of shared workspaces.
Use separate non-sensitive demo files for cross-tool workflows.
Clear clipboard after transferring content.
Disable or avoid opening confidential screenshots/files in ChatGPT Desktop during Cursor sessions.

C_capability_conflict.rationale: Cursor has write_filesystem, modify_git_state, and broad network egress; ChatGPT Desktop can read files and interact with connected IDE content and clipboard. In a shared project, B can mutate the same codebase A is inspecting, and Cursor’s Yolo mode can auto-run commands. That makes conflicting writes and git-state races dangerous by default.
conditions: IF both agents operate on the same repository, concurrent edits can conflict.
IF Cursor Yolo mode is enabled, unreviewed writes can race with ChatGPT Desktop-guided changes.
mitigations: Pause one agent before the other edits the repo.
Use separate branches for each agent.
Turn off Cursor Yolo mode.
Commit or stash before switching agents.
Restrict both agents to read-only review on the same task.

D_cascading_error.rationale: ChatGPT Desktop can produce analysis from files, screenshots, and connected IDEs, and Cursor’s agent loop can act on those outputs with tool use and auto-run commands. That creates a default pathway where A’s output becomes B’s operational input without a mandatory verification step. Because B can execute shell and modify git state, downstream mistakes can become real actions.
conditions: IF Cursor consumes ChatGPT Desktop recommendations as authoritative, errors cascade into code or shell actions.
IF ChatGPT Desktop summarizes files incorrectly and Cursor executes the summary, the mistake propagates.
mitigations: Require human review before any Cursor action.
Ask Cursor to verify ChatGPT Desktop claims against source files.
Disable auto-run/Yolo mode.
Use a checklist for any shell or git operation.
Limit ChatGPT Desktop to advisory-only outputs.

E_compliance.rationale: Both profiles are closed-source and docs-only, but the visible compliance issue is mainly a retention/residency mismatch risk rather than a proven breach. A handles uploaded files and screenshots through OpenAI-managed services; B sends content to model providers and MCP servers. The profiles do not specify a concrete residency conflict, so low is appropriate.
conditions: IF regulated data is sent through both vendors without a DPA review, compliance gaps may arise.
IF retention settings differ across the two services for the same data class, policy mismatch occurs.
mitigations: Avoid regulated data in cross-tool workflows.
Review vendor retention settings before use.
Document which data classes may enter each tool.
Use synthetic data for shared tasks.
